questions.prompt: What can Defender for Identity detect that endpoint EDR structurally cannot?
options: Activity from an unmanaged host with no EDR agent, because the sensor sits on the domain controller where the authentication actually happens
questions.explanation: Because detection occurs at the authentication and directory layer rather than the endpoint, an attacker operating from a machine with no agent is still visible when they talk to a DC.

questions.prompt: Why are there multiple distinct Golden Ticket alert variants?
options: It is a product bug generating duplicates

Each corresponds to a different anomaly in a forged ticket -- a nonexistent account, an implausible lifetime, inconsistent authorization data -- so which one fired tells you something about how it was forged
Each covers a different Windows version
They fire in sequence as the attack progresses
questions.explanation: The variants are distinct tells rather than duplicates, and identifying which anomaly triggered narrows how the forgery was constructed.

questions.prompt: What makes a honeytoken account such a high-signal detection?
options: It is never used legitimately, so any authentication involving it is actionable without further correlation
questions.explanation: This is the inverse of break-glass alerting -- an account that exists only to be watched, producing essentially zero false positives.

questions.prompt: Why does an alert not replace understanding the underlying technique?
options: An alert names a technique but does not investigate it -- a DCSync alert still requires reading 4662 events, establishing which account, when rights were granted, and what else was touched
questions.explanation: The product is a detection layer over techniques an analyst still needs to understand, which is why this content follows Level 4 rather than substituting for it.
